title: Meeting Report: Pharmaceuticals in Water, An Interdisciplinary Approach to a Public Health Challenge (Rodriguez-Mozaz & Weinberg, Environmental Health Perspectives 2010)
source: Sara Rodriguez-Mozaz and Howard S. Weinberg, Environmental Health Perspectives 118:1016–1020 (2010); assigned from the beginning up to the section “Best management practices”
lecture: Assigned for 10/9; discussed in class 10/13 with the discussion guide
about: A review of how medications reach ground water, surface water and drinking water and what is known about their effects. The body metabolizes only part of a prescribed drug, so unchanged drug and metabolites leave in human waste and travel through wastewater into streams, lakes and the water that drinking-water plants use (p. 1016). Wastewater treatment plants are the main point where these drugs enter surface water, because their treatment steps were not designed to remove pharmaceuticals; some drugs collect in biosolids sold as fertilizer; farm animals receive drugs directly in feed (p. 1017). People take the drugs in mainly by mouth through drinking water (p. 1018). The assigned portion stops before the best-management-practices section.

listen: This reading is the article "Meeting Report: Pharmaceuticals in Water, An Interdisciplinary Approach to a Public Health Challenge," by Sara Rodriguez Mozaz and Howard Weinberg, in Environmental Health Perspectives, 2010. It reports an environmental health summit of government agencies, academics, industry and other scientists. The part before Best Management Practices illustrates the five principles of toxicology, for humans and for wildlife. As her quiz keyed them, the five are source, exposure, A D M E T, dose, and target and mechanism of action. Source. Her key lists flushing, which could be reduced by other disposal methods. Animal waste could be reduced by controls on feedlots and farms. Human waste can't be reduced, because people take medications. Wildlife has the same sources. The greatest source is consumption of medications by humans and the resulting waste streams. Of treatment plants she said, "the current mechanisms don't get all the drugs out of it before it goes back into your streams and rivers and lakes." Exposure. For humans the routes are drinking water, eating fish, and skin contact during recreation. Duration and frequency depend on how people are exposed and where they live. She said the concentrations are "about parts per trillion." For wildlife the routes are drinking water, food, and skin. Exposure is repeated and lasts their entire life. It is constant if their home range stays contaminated. Her key says aquatic wildlife exposure is the more significant one. A D M E. For humans there are some data from drug development studies. For wildlife there is very little if any data, because the studies have not been done. Dose. For both, the real dose is unknown, because values often were not measured, were undetected, or were modeled. The human dose is probably below the therapeutic dose. She asked, "is that gonna get you up to a normal therapeutic daily dose? No, no." So it is false that the drinking water dose exceeds the therapeutic daily dose. For wildlife, the doses that cause harm are unknown, but given their exposure, their dose is likely high enough to cause effects. Target and mechanism. For humans we don't know the effects of low dose chronic exposure, we lack data on sensitive populations, the fetus, children, the elderly, and people with disease, and we don't know how multiple exposures act. For wildlife we don't always know the organ affected, the data may come from the wrong species or the wrong endpoint, and multiple exposures are unknown. She described frogs, fish and alligators "changing from being like half male, half female to more female in those places where estrogen levels are higher." The authors' conclusion: more data is needed to determine whether pharmaceuticals in water harm human health. Asked whether wildlife is being harmed, one student said yes and one said we don't know, and she said, "you're both right." The traps. The greatest source is human use and waste, not flushing, landfills, or manufacturing. Flushing can be reduced, but human waste cannot. Wildlife is exposed constantly and for life.
